title: Bluetooth Race Car
goal: A beginner-buildable, battery-powered, two-motor differential-drive race car controlled over Bluetooth LE.

requirements.label: Two independently controlled brushed DC motors
Hobbyist prototype build with boards and modules

outputV.note: Single 5 V rail shared by the XIAO VBUS input and the motor driver

assumptions.reason: 3S instead of the handoff's 2S: with a series Schottky and a 5 V LM2596 output, 2S leaves under 1 V of regulator headroom at end of discharge. 3S keeps about 4 V. Exact pack and connector deferred.
Simple, through-hole, protects the buck and everything downstream; costs about 0.45 V that 3S can afford
One buck output feeds both the XIAO 5V input and the driver motor rail. Motors are 6 V nominal, so this trades roughly 17 percent top speed for one regulator.
Heuristic bulk capacitance on the shared 5 V rail to soften motor start and stall transients. Not a component-spec invariant.
Per motor, averaged over a mixed drive cycle at about 40 percent duty. Runtime estimate depends on this.
XIAO ESP32-S3 with BLE active, no Wi-Fi
Typical for an LM2596 module at this ratio and load

assumptions.value: D0-D5 to PWMA, AIN1, AIN2, PWMB, BIN1, BIN2; D6 to STBY
assumptions.reason: Arbitrary; any PWM-capable XIAO GPIO works

designGuide.summary: A 3S battery feeds a protected, regulated power path. The XIAO ESP32-S3 handles the Bluetooth link and sends low-current control signals to the TB6612 motor driver, which switches and reverses the larger motor current for the two gearmotors, so each side of the car can be driven on its own for steering.

flow.label: Battery
flow.explanation: Three LiPo cells in series, about {{battery.nominal_v}} V when nominal and falling toward {{battery.min_usable_v}} V as they discharge. Everything else in the car runs from this pack.

flow.label: Protection
flow.explanation: The Schottky diode passes current only in the right direction, so a pack plugged in backwards pushes nothing into the rest of the circuit. It costs about {{diode.forward_drop_v}} V of the battery voltage.

flow.label: Regulation
flow.explanation: The LM2596 buck module steps the battery voltage down to the {{assumption.motor_rail_v}} V rail that powers both the controller and the motors. The bulk capacitor on that rail steadies it when the motors draw a sudden gulp of current.

flow.label: Controller
flow.explanation: The XIAO ESP32-S3 runs the software and the Bluetooth LE link. It powers itself from the 5 V rail, makes its own 3.3 V, and drives seven pins on the motor driver: for each motor, one speed signal (PWM, a fast on/off pulse whose on-time sets the speed) and two direction signals, plus one standby line that keeps the driver switched on.

flow.label: Motor driver
flow.explanation: The TB6612 holds two H-bridges: four switches around each motor that let current be sent through it in either direction. It reads the XIAO's logic signals and switches the 5 V motor supply: forward, reverse, or brake per motor, with speed set by how long the PWM signal is on. Its logic side runs from the XIAO's 3.3 V.

flow.label: Left and right motors
flow.explanation: Each gearmotor spins at a speed set by the voltage across it and reverses when the driver swaps its two terminals. Driving the two sides at different speeds or directions steers the car.

paths.power: Battery → diode → buck module → 5 V rail → XIAO and motor driver. The motors draw from the 5 V rail through the driver; the XIAO's onboard regulator makes 3.3 V for its own logic and for the driver's logic side.
paths.control: Bluetooth LE → XIAO software → seven logic pins → TB6612 inputs → the driver's two H-bridges → motors. Only low-current logic signals leave the controller; the driver does the heavy switching.
paths.outcome: Two independently driven wheels: the same direction and speed on both goes straight, different speeds turn, opposite directions spin in place. The rules check that this hardware path exists; what the software does with the link and the signals is not evaluated.

parts.why: Provides the energy. Three cells give the regulator enough headroom to hold 5 V all the way to the pack's cutoff, which is why the design uses 3S rather than 2S.
A hobbyist build gets plugged in backwards eventually. This diode makes that a non-event instead of a dead board, for about {{diode.forward_drop_v}} V and one part.
The motors and the XIAO both want about 5 V, not the pack's 9.6 to 12.6 V. The buck makes that rail efficiently, so little of the battery's energy is lost as heat.
Motors starting or stalling pull sudden current. This reservoir keeps the 5 V rail from sagging in those moments. Its size is a rule of thumb, not a calculated value.

Runs the control software and the Bluetooth link, and produces the direction and speed signals. It cannot drive the motors itself: a pin can source only about {{mcu.gpio_max_source_current_a}} A and cannot reverse the current through a motor.

Turns the XIAO's signals into motor current, up to {{driver.continuous_current_per_channel_a}} A per channel continuously, and reverses each motor on command. Without it there is no forward and reverse, and the XIAO would be damaged trying.
Converts electrical power into wheel motion on the left side.
Converts electrical power into wheel motion on the right side. Two motors driven independently give steering with no steering mechanism at all.

decisions.title: Why a separate motor driver, instead of wiring the motors to the XIAO?
decisions.explanation: A microcontroller pin is a signal, not a power source: it can source only about {{mcu.gpio_max_source_current_a}} A, and it can only push current out, never pull it back the other way through a motor. Each motor can draw up to {{motor_left.stall_current_a}} A (its rated stall current at 6 V) when stalled and has to run in both directions. An H-bridge driver switches that current from the motor rail and reverses it under logic control; the TB6612 has two, one per motor. Try "What if a motor is wired to a GPIO?" under Try a change to see the rule that catches the shortcut.

decisions.title: Why a 3S battery and a regulator, rather than running everything from the pack?
decisions.explanation: The motors are rated {{motor_left.nominal_v}} V and the XIAO takes 5 V on its supply pin, so the pack's 9.6 to 12.6 V cannot feed either directly. A buck module makes a steady {{assumption.motor_rail_v}} V rail from it. The buck needs its input to stay about {{buck.dropout_v}} V above its output, so roughly 6.5 V, and the protection diode takes another {{diode.forward_drop_v}} V before that, so the pack must stay above about 7 V. A 3S pack is still at {{battery.min_usable_v}} V at its cutoff, with margin to spare; a 2S pack's cutoff sits below that line, so it runs out of headroom before it runs out of charge. Try "What if the battery is 2S?" under Try a change to see the warning.

decisions.title: Why run 6 V motors from the 5 V rail?
decisions.explanation: One shared {{assumption.motor_rail_v}} V rail keeps the design to a single regulator that feeds both the controller and the motors. The motors are rated {{motor_left.nominal_v}} V, so at 5 V they run below their rated speed and torque; the evaluation estimates how much, from the rating, not from a measurement. That is the tradeoff: a simpler power path against some top speed. The optimization below shows the alternative: a 6 V motor rail plus a second regulator so the controller's supply stays in range.

decisions.title: Why include reverse-polarity protection?
decisions.explanation: A series Schottky costs about {{diode.forward_drop_v}} V of battery voltage and one part. In exchange, a pack connected backwards simply does nothing, instead of forcing reverse voltage into the buck and everything behind it. This pack class is assumed to have no reverse protection of its own. Dropping the diode is the optimization below: fewer parts and a little more headroom, and one wiring mistake becomes destructive.

decisions.title: Why can the battery be smaller?
decisions.explanation: The runtime target is 15 to 30 minutes. With the assumed average motor current of {{assumption.avg_motor_current_a}} A per motor and controller current of {{assumption.mcu_avg_current_a}} A, a {{battery.capacity_mah_min}} mAh pack runs roughly six times longer than the target, and that unused capacity is mass and cost on a small car. The optimization below swaps in a 200 to 300 mAh 3S pack with the same voltage window and the same protection. The estimate moves because the assumed inputs moved, not because anything was measured.

mutations.label: What if there is no battery?
mutations.description: Deletes the battery instance and clears the power source. The project becomes incomplete and voltage-dependent rules stop evaluating.

mutations.label: What if the driver's ground is broken?
mutations.description: Moves the driver GND pin onto its own net. The driver still receives 5 V and control signals but shares no reference with the XIAO.

mutations.label: What if STBY is tied to ground?
mutations.description: Moves the driver STBY pin from the XIAO GPIO to GND. The driver is held in standby.

mutations.label: What if STBY is left unconnected?
mutations.description: Disconnects STBY entirely. On this exact Adafruit breakout the 10 kOhm pull-up keeps the driver enabled, so no finding is expected.

mutations.label: What if a motor is wired to a GPIO?
mutations.description: Moves the left motor off the driver and onto XIAO D7 and D8.

mutations.label: What if the buck is set to 3.3 V?
mutations.description: Changes the buck module output. The driver motor supply minimum is 4.5 V and the XIAO 5V input expects about 5 V.

mutations.label: What if the buck is set to 14 V?
mutations.description: Exceeds the driver's 13.5 V motor supply maximum and the XIAO 5V input.

mutations.label: Remove reverse-polarity protection
mutations.description: Deletes the diode and wires the battery straight into the buck. The circuit still runs; the reverse-polarity strategy is gone.

mutations.label: Remove the bulk capacitor
mutations.description: Deletes the 470 uF capacitor from the 5 V rail. Heuristic rule; expect a warning, not a failure.

mutations.label: What if the battery is 2S?
mutations.description: Uses the handoff's original 2S class. With the series diode, the buck sees about 5.95 V at end of discharge for a 5 V output.

mutations.label: What if a motor stalls at 2.5 A?
mutations.description: Replaces the left motor with a class whose stall current exceeds the driver's 1.2 A continuous limit.

mutations.label: What if the driver is a bare IC?
mutations.description: Replaces the Adafruit breakout with the bare Toshiba IC. Same limits, but no onboard decoupling and no STBY pull-up.

mutations.label: What if a bare TB6612 has STBY floating?
mutations.description: Swaps in the bare IC and leaves STBY unconnected. The bare chip has no pull-up, so the enable state is unknown rather than fine.

mutations.label: What if the buck is set to 10 V?
mutations.description: Above the battery's cutoff voltage minus the diode drop: a buck cannot step up, so the setting can never be reached.

mutations.label: What if the Schottky is installed backwards?
mutations.description: Swaps the diode's anode and cathode nets. A reversed series diode blocks normal current and conducts when the battery is reversed.

mutations.label: What if the B channel inputs are left off?
mutations.description: Disconnects BIN1 and BIN2 while MOTORB1 and MOTORB2 stay wired to the right motor. The driver's B outputs have no direction inputs, so the right motor cannot be driven.

optimizations.title: Right-size the battery for the runtime target
optimizations.goal: 15 to 30 minute runtime with the smallest, lightest pack that meets it
optimizations.summary: Swaps the 1000-1500 mAh 3S class for a 200-300 mAh 3S class. Same voltage window, same protection, about a quarter of the mass.
acceptsRisks: Less reserve if the average-current assumption is optimistic

optimizations.title: Run the motors at their rated 6 V
optimizations.goal: Top speed and torque the motors are rated for
optimizations.summary: Raises the motor rail to 6 V and adds a second LM2596 module set to 5 V for the XIAO, so the logic supply stays inside its range.
acceptsRisks: One more module to wire and adjust
Higher stall current at 6 V; driver margin shrinks

optimizations.title: Drop the reverse-polarity diode
optimizations.summary: Removes the 1N5822 and wires the battery straight into the buck. The car runs the same; one reversed battery connection is no longer protected against.
acceptsRisks: A reversed battery connection puts full pack voltage backwards across the buck and everything after it
